CQA_f96f9611709a6cf3.question: How does the interpretation of the location parameter as both a quantile and a distributional characteristic differ when the skewness parameter is fixed versus when it is modeled as a function of covariates, and what does this imply for studying covariate effects on central tendency?
CQA_f96f9611709a6cf3.answer: When the skewness parameter τ is fixed at a predetermined quantile order (as in LQMM and LSLQMM), the location parameter μ_ij corresponds exactly to the τth quantile of the conditional distribution, meaning μ_ij directly represents a specific position in the probability distribution chosen a priori. When τ_ij is instead modeled as a function of covariates and random effects via logit(τ_ij) = x'_{ij,τ}α + z'_{ij,τ}a_i (as in ALDRM), the location parameter μ_ij becomes the mode of the distribution, and its identity as the τ_ijth quantile becomes data-driven rather than investigator-specified. This distinction has critical implications for interpreting covariate effects on central tendency: in the fixed-τ approach, a covariate effect on the location parameter β represents its impact on a predetermined quantile (e.g., median when τ=0.5), while in the modeled-τ approach, covariate effects on β represent impacts on the mode—the most probable value—which may shift independently of how asymmetry changes. Furthermore, in ALDRM, covariates can affect central tendency through both the location component (directly via β) and the skewness component (indirectly via α, since the mean equals μ + σ(1-2τ)/(τ(1-τ))). The GMQ smoothing approach inherently assumes fixed τ to define which quantile is being estimated, achieving √n-consistency with bias O(c²|ln c|) for that specific quantile, whereas the distributional regression approach with modeled τ provides a complete characterization of how the entire distribution's shape—including which quantile corresponds to the mode—changes with covariates.
CQA_f96f9611709a6cf3.relation: Paper 1 defines the location parameter as the quantile of a fixed order τ in quantile regression; Paper 2 defines it as the mode when τ is modeled, creating an apparent conflict in interpretation that must be resolved by understanding when the mode equals a quantile and how this relationship changes when τ varies with covariates.
CQA_f96f9611709a6cf3.derived_conclusion: The location parameter serves dual roles: as a pre-specified quantile when τ is fixed (enabling targeted quantile regression) versus as the mode when τ is estimated (enabling distributional modeling). Covariate effects on central tendency are unambiguous only in the fixed-τ case; when τ varies with covariates, the distinction between effects on the mode, median, mean, and other quantiles must be explicitly computed using the AL distribution's closed-form relationships.

The empirical estimator β̂(τ) for quantile regression is obtained by minimizing (1/n)Σρ_τ(y_i - x'_i β(τ)), targeting a specific quantile of order τ

For the AL distribution with parameters (μ, σ, τ), the location parameter μ corresponds to both the mode and the quantile of order τ
The quantile of order p for Y ~ AL(μ, σ, τ) is Q_Y(p) = μ + σ/(1-τ)·log(p/τ) if p≤τ, and μ - σ/τ·log((1-p)/(1-τ)) if p>τ
The expectation of Y ~ AL(μ, σ, τ) is E(Y) = μ + σ(1-2τ)/(τ(1-τ)), showing the mean differs from the mode μ when τ≠0.5

In ALDRM, the skewness parameter is modeled as logit(τ_ij) = x'_{ij,τ}α + z'_{ij,τ}a_i, making τ vary with covariates and random effects, so the mode μ_ij corresponds to the data-driven quantile of order τ_ij

CQA_400ca29a206ad318.answer: In both cases, optimal performance is achieved by maximizing the pairwise separation between the events the receiver must distinguish, and each paper shows this separation directly controls the rate at which residual uncertainty vanishes. In the OCPC, the analogous separation is combinatorial rather than metric: the optimal code construction (proof of Theorem 7) shows that any code with overlapping band-usage regions W_S (|S|>=2, used by more than one message) can be replaced by a code with disjoint regions U_k without increasing error probability, i.e., the optimal code assigns each message its own band exclusively. So while the Gaussian channel's separation criterion is a continuous minimum-distance constraint (yielding an exponential-in-snr rate), the OCPC's separation criterion is complete disjointness of resource regions (yielding an exact, no-overlap optimal code); both are the operative 'native' mechanism by which each paper's optimal scheme suppresses residual receiver ambiguity.

CQA_9439af39674dd162.question: In both PnP-PGD under prior mismatch and the ARWP sampling method, the exact target operator (the true MMSE denoiser and the true score function) is replaced by a tractable surrogate, introducing a bias term. How does each paper's own surrogate-induced bias term behave asymptotically, and what mechanism does each provide to keep that bias from dominating convergence?
CQA_9439af39674dd162.answer: In PnP-PGD, replacing the target MMSE denoiser D_sigma by a mismatched denoiser bar-D_sigma introduces per-iteration error epsilon_k, and Theorem 2.1 shows the gradient-norm bound depends on the partial sums of epsilon_k; if {epsilon_k} is summable (e.g. epsilon_k = O(1/k^{1+delta})), the bound vanishes and PnP-PGD converges exactly to a stationary point despite the mismatch (Lemma 2.1, Theorem 2.1). Equivariant averaging (EPnP) further shrinks this error deterministically at every iteration, since the equivariant bias satisfies epsilon_tilde_k = epsilon_hat_k − Var_g < epsilon_hat_k whenever the underlying bias is anisotropic (Lemma 2.2, Theorem 2.3), tightening the same bound without retraining. In ARWP, replacing the true score ∇log ρ_t with ∇log WProx_{T,V}ρ_t introduces a bias that depends only on the regularization parameter T (not on step-size η) and does not vanish with more iterations; instead the terminal stationary covariance Σ_∞ satisfies WProx_{T,V}(N(0,Σ_∞)) = N(0,Λ), i.e. the method converges to a T-dependent biased fixed point rather than the exact target unless T→0. Thus PnP-PGD's mismatch bias is an iteration-decaying error controllable to zero via a summability condition (or reduced via equivariance), whereas ARWP's regularization bias is a persistent, tunable floor fixed by the choice of T.

CQA_257668dc296ccc7e.question: Both papers prove existence for a coupled system by first isolating a lower-dimensional subproblem that decouples from the rest. What is the decoupled component in each paper's construction, and why does isolating it make the overall existence proof tractable?
CQA_257668dc296ccc7e.answer: In the UBI paper, the (I+1)-dimensional quadratic BSDE system (3.2) is coupled, but the scalar (a, Z_a) equation decouples from the Y_i equations (the coupling that remains is not quadratic). This lets the authors first solve (a, Z_a) via a truncation argument (Tevzadze-type results) to get a bounded solution, and then treat each (Y_i, Z_i) as a one-dimensional linear BSDE solvable by existing linear BSDE theory (Jackson-Žitković), avoiding having to solve the full coupled quadratic system directly. In the MMOT paper, the dual problem (D) over potentials (u,h) is handled by first establishing a constructive feasible (Slater) point P_0 with density bounded between m' and M' (Lemma 3.2), which decouples the feasibility question from the optimization itself; this Slater point is what allows Fenchel-Rockafellar duality to be invoked cleanly, guaranteeing no duality gap and existence/uniqueness of the primal-dual pair (Theorem 3.1). In both cases, the strategy is the same: solve/verify a simpler, isolated auxiliary object first (a scalar decoupled BSDE, or a strictly-bounded-density feasible point) so that standard existence machinery (linear BSDE theory, Fenchel-Rockafellar) applies to the remaining coupled optimization.

CQA_43d186ae24c67a13.question: Both survey experiments report small standardized effect sizes for their attitude-shifting manipulations. How do the two studies differ in benchmarking the practical significance of these small effects, and what general lesson does this suggest for interpreting small Cohen's d values in policy-attitude experiments?
CQA_43d186ae24c67a13.answer: In the migration study, the Dutch-blame treatment produces effects of negligible magnitude versus control (d < 0.2) and negligible-to-small magnitude versus the US-blame condition (0.1 < d < 0.3); the authors explicitly conclude that although statistically significant, these effects are 'small in practical terms' and offer no external yardstick for what such a d actually means for policy outcomes. The psilocybin study reports comparably small effects on policy support (d = 0.10–0.11) but supplies an implementation-relevant benchmark: it notes that a roughly 9-percentage-point increase in support for prescription-based legalization is associated with an estimated 8% increase in the odds of policy implementation, drawing on external meta-analytic evidence linking support gains to adoption likelihood. Reconciling the two studies shows that a small Cohen's d (roughly 0.1–0.3) in an attitude-shifting experiment cannot be judged 'negligible' or 'practically important' in the abstract; its practical weight depends on whether the researchers can map the support shift onto a real-world implementation-probability metric, something the psilocybin study does and the migration study does not.

The psilocybin study instead runs two-way ANCOVAs in which the pre-intervention (baseline) measurement of the same outcome (policy support or belief) is entered as the covariate, because its design includes a pre-test and post-test for every respondent. CQA_0c67dae3274dbf73.question: Both papers report a discrete 'all-or-nothing' failure phenomenon rather than smooth degradation when redundant resources fall below a critical amount. CQA_0c67dae3274dbf73.answer: In NBQC, the Clos-network node count experiences discrete jumps whenever the number of internal or external ports crosses a power of the switch-size parameter s (i.e., increases from s^k to s^k+1); this happens because Clos switches are built recursively from perfect bipartite blocks, so a small increase in port count that crosses a s^k boundary forces the construction of an entirely new tier of switches, sharply increasing node count even though execution-time requirements changed only marginally. In UAV-CPN, when the fuel energy budget E_fuel falls at or below 42,000 J under the static configuration h=100 m, P_d=10 dBW, task completion probability collapses completely to zero rather than degrading gradually, because that altitude/power pair's propulsion energy demand exceeds the available fuel outright, making the configuration entirely infeasible (accounting for 40% of tested energy-budget combinations). In both cases the underlying cause is a hard structural/physical constraint (switch-block boundary vs. absolute energy exhaustion) rather than a continuous resource-performance trade-off, which is why neither system shows smooth scaling near these critical points; NBQC's Clos Network Optimization subroutine can remove the resulting excess nodes without changing execution time, whereas UAV-CPN's fixed static configuration has no such recovery mechanism and instead requires switching to the joint altitude-power optimization strategy to avoid the infeasible region.

CQA_e887d3f3410e5ae1.question: Both papers reduce an intractable joint resource-allocation problem to a sequence of tractable subproblems solved heuristically/iteratively rather than exactly. Compare NBQC's node-reduction optimization strategy to UAV-CPN's alternating iterative joint optimization, and explain what property each gives up to gain tractability.
CQA_e887d3f3410e5ae1.answer: NBQC's optimization loop (NBQC Construction, Clos Network Optimization, Bottleneck Identification, Update NBQC Configuration) tackles the NP-hard problem of minimizing switching-network nodes subject to a fixed execution time by converting middle-switch assignment into a graph vertex-coloring problem and solving it with the greedy Welsh-Powell algorithm, explicitly sacrificing global optimality (the construction does not guarantee the optimal solution and may need many iterations) in exchange for a fast, near-optimal, incrementally updatable network. UAV-CPN's Algorithm 1 similarly decomposes the joint optimization of continuous altitude h and transmit power P_d into an alternating two-stage scheme, using golden-section search for altitude and a quasi-Newton method for transmit power, which converts the 2D joint search into sequential 1D optimizations; this sacrifices the full-space search performed by exact/Bayesian methods, trading some solution quality (in fact UAV-CPN's own comparison shows alternating optimization outperforms a Bayesian-optimization baseline in 69.2% of scenarios given equal evaluation budgets specifically because reduced dimensionality yields denser sampling) for linear time complexity O(T*N) rather than searching the full joint parameter space. Thus both papers accept a heuristic, dimensionality-reducing approach (discrete graph coloring in NBQC; alternating 1D search in UAV-CPN) instead of solving the underlying combinatorial or continuous joint optimization exactly, prioritizing scalability to large node counts or large user populations over guaranteed optimality.

A complete answer about the shared strategy of trading optimality for tractability must draw on both specific heuristic mechanisms.
CQA_e887d3f3410e5ae1.derived_conclusion: Both papers independently adopt a decomposition-based heuristic (discrete graph coloring vs. alternating continuous search) that reduces a jointly-coupled, high-dimensional resource optimization problem to sequential lower-dimensional subproblems, accepting near-optimal rather than globally optimal solutions in exchange for practical, scalable runtime.

CQA_678ebe128c9fe565.question: Both NBQC and the UAV-enabled Computing Power Network (UAV-CPN) framework define a condition under which a slow resource becomes the dominant limiter of end-to-end performance. How does each paper formalize this threshold, and what does comparing them reveal about whether adding redundant resources can actually remove the bottleneck in each system?
CQA_678ebe128c9fe565.answer: In NBQC, a qubit component is 'bottleneck-free' only if its ring network is long enough that the round-trip time n_ring(d-1)T_local exceeds the Bell-pair regeneration latency T_Bell, so the algorithmic qubit always finds a freshly distilled entanglement link when it needs to move or communicate; if the ring is too short, the qubit stalls waiting for entanglement regeneration, and the 'Bottleneck Identification' subroutine explicitly measures this wait time w^QQ/w^QF to find where more QQ/QF links (redundant nodes) are needed. In UAV-CPN, task failure is instead defined by two disjoint threshold conditions: a 'comm-limited' regime, where the combined offload/forward transmission time t1+t2 already exceeds the latency budget T_max regardless of a chosen computing node, and a 'comp-limited' regime, where the computing latency t_c exceeds the residual budget T_res = T_max - t1 - t2. In both papers, redundancy resolves the bottleneck only when it targets the correct constraint: NBQC's node redundancy is a topological fix (adding channels/links extends ring length and increases entanglement supply), whereas UAV-CPN's 'redundancy' (higher CN density, wider service zone, or altitude/power tuning) only helps if it enlarges the effective communication radius r_c^max(r_u) or raises the CDF F_tc(T_res;D); redundant CNs beyond the latency-constrained radius, or extra nodes in an already sufficiently long NBQC ring, do not reduce the respective bottleneck.

Explaining the shared 'threshold that separates concealed-latency from exposed-latency regimes' concept requires both formal thresholds side by side.

CQA_8d2edb7067c13297.answer: Paper 1 addresses 'results of a cause'—examining how randomized interventions (communicating benefits and safety information) affect policy support outcomes. Paper 2 explains (page 21) that regression analysis is designed to 'estimate the average causal effect' and suits questions about 'the result of a given cause,' while QCA is designed to 'explore the configurational conditions under which an outcome occurs' and suits questions about 'the cause of a result.' Paper 1's 2×2 factorial design with random assignment (page 2) creates independent experimental manipulation of two interventions, making it optimal for estimating treatment effects. Paper 2 states (page 21) regression 'implies an assumption of probabilistic causality' with error terms capturing unobserved factors, fitting Paper 1's goal of estimating average intervention impacts. QCA would become appropriate if Paper 1 instead asked which configurations of respondent characteristics (demographics, prior beliefs) lead to policy acceptance, but Paper 1's focus on manipulated treatment effects aligns with regression's framework rather than QCA's configurational logic for analyzing naturally occurring condition combinations.

CQA_8d2edb7067c13297.answer_pre_raw:
Paper 1's factorial experiment (2x2 Benefits x Safety manipulation, testing whether each intervention increases policy support/beliefs, analyzed via two-way ANCOVA) addresses "results of a given cause" questions — i.e., estimating the net average effect of a specified, randomly-assigned cause (each information intervention) on an outcome (policy support/beliefs), holding the other factor and baseline covariate constant. This matches Paper 2's framework of quantitative/regression-style causal analysis, which focuses on estimating the average net effect of X on Y after eliminating confounders, rather than the qualitative "causes of a given result" question (identifying which configurations of conditions are necessary/sufficient to produce an observed outcome in individual cases).

ANCOVA is appropriate for Paper 1 because: (1) the intervention structure is a factorial design with only two independent, orthogonally manipulated binary causes (Benefits info vs. no info; Safety info vs. no info), randomized between-subjects, so causal identification of each factor's net effect (and their two-way interaction) is straightforward and low-dimensional; (2) the design includes a continuous pre-test covariate (baseline policy support/beliefs) that ANCOVA can statistically control for, increasing precision; (3) outcomes are continuous 7-point scale ratings, suited to a linear/additive symmetric model estimating mean differences (Cohen's d).

This same structure limits applicability of QCA (Paper 2's configurational approach): QCA is designed for situations with multiple (typically many, categorical/fuzzy) causal conditions whose combinations (configurations) jointly and asymmetrically produce an outcome across heterogeneous cases, capturing equifinality and necessary/sufficient conditions distinguishing presence vs. absence of the outcome. Paper 1 has only two manipulated binary factors (not the multi-condition configurational profiles QCA needs), the two interventions are independently and randomly assigned (not naturally covarying "recipes" of conditions to be uncovered), the outcome is a continuous scale rather than a set-membership/dichotomous outcome, and the goal is estimating the isolated net effect of each information type on support (a "results of a cause" question) rather than explaining diverse case-level configurational pathways to a given outcome (a "causes of a result" question) — the latter being QCA's strength, as demonstrated in Paper 2's mate-preference analysis.

CQA_49292df195903c99.question: Paper 1 found that for safety beliefs, both the Benefits intervention and Safety intervention had significant main effects, but post-hoc tests revealed each intervention increased safety beliefs only when the other intervention was absent—when both were present together, neither showed significant effects. According to Paper 2's explanation of configurational causality and regression limitations, why does this pattern represent the type of complex conditional relationship that QCA's approach could characterize more explicitly than Paper 1's interaction term analysis?
CQA_49292df195903c99.answer: This represents configurational causality because the effectiveness of each intervention depends on the specific combination with the other intervention—a non-additive relationship where single interventions work but their combination does not. Paper 1 found (page 5) that Benefits intervention significantly increased safety beliefs only when Safety intervention was absent (F=80.89, p<.001), and Safety intervention increased safety beliefs only when Benefits was absent (F=99.61, p<.001), but when both were received, effects became non-significant. Paper 2 explains (page 10) that regression 'estimates the net effect of a specific criterion after controlling for all other variables' which 'does not align with how mate selection decisions are actually made' when conditions work together. Paper 2 states (page 14) configurational analysis examines 'combinations of multiple causes' and that 'it is the configuration of these conditions, rather than any single condition, that truly exerts influence.' QCA would explicitly model this as two distinct sufficient configurations (Benefits AND NOT Safety) OR (NOT Benefits AND Safety) leading to increased safety beliefs, versus (Benefits AND Safety) not leading to the outcome, making the conditional dependencies transparent rather than representing them through a single interaction coefficient.
CQA_49292df195903c99.relation: Paper 1 provides empirical evidence of a complex non-additive interaction pattern where combined interventions lose effectiveness; Paper 2 provides the conceptual framework explaining why such patterns exemplify configurational causality better captured through set-theoretic methods
CQA_49292df195903c99.derived_conclusion: Paper 1's finding that single interventions are effective but their combination is not represents configurational causality where specific condition combinations determine outcomes, which Paper 2's QCA framework would model more explicitly through set-theoretic representations than regression's single interaction term

Regression analysis obtains the estimated net effect of a specific criterion after controlling for all other variables, ignoring interactive relationships among mate selection criteria and not aligning with how decisions are actually made when multiple characteristics are evaluated simultaneously

In configurational analysis, what primarily influences decision-making is the consideration of various attributes together rather than any single criterion in isolation; such combinations of causal conditions are referred to as configurations, and in the experimental design profiles incorporated all characteristics simultaneously so it is the configuration that truly exerts influence

CQA_a0e82d6a06c98182.question: Does the frequency-dependent multibanding scheme used to accelerate ROQ basis construction rest on an assumption about orbital eccentricity that is challenged by the population of known binary pulsars?
CQA_a0e82d6a06c98182.answer: Yes. The multibanding scheme is derived from the circular-orbit time-frequency relation t(f) = 5(8πf)^(-8/3) M_c^(-5/3), which assumes signal power accumulates smoothly at each frequency according to chirp mass alone, justifying coarser sampling at high frequency. Paper 2 shows that for eccentric binary pulsars, gravitational-wave power is emitted at multiple harmonics of the orbital frequency and is enhanced by the eccentricity factor F(e) = (1+73/24 e^2+37/96 e^4)/(1-e^2)^(7/2) relative to a circular orbit of the same semi-major axis, and that higher eccentricity concentrates emission near periastron. This means the amount of signal power and cycles present at a given frequency for an eccentric pulsar-like source would not follow the circular t(f) scaling that the multiband spacing is built on, so the specific band boundaries and frequency-doubling structure derived for the aligned-spin, effectively circularized SSM waveform would not automatically preserve accuracy if applied to eccentric sources without modification.
CQA_a0e82d6a06c98182.relation: Paper 1 supplies the circular-orbit time-frequency scaling underlying the multiband construction, and Paper 2 supplies the eccentricity-dependent enhancement factor showing how real binary pulsar emission departs from that circular scaling; both are needed to assess whether the multibanding rule generalizes.
CQA_a0e82d6a06c98182.derived_conclusion: The multibanding rule as formulated is tied to circular-orbit inspiral timing and would need modification to remain accurate for eccentric sources of the kind found among binary pulsars.

CQA_362808d2bade8395.question: The vcFLE paper shows the transition amplitude Tj=Aj|+/Aj|- =1 for each soliton across a collision, while the mKdV paper shows that when a=u_m^2 stays constant, the DSW's small-amplitude edge moves with constant velocity dxl/dt=-12a. Explain why each result is naturally stated as invariance of a different physical quantity (amplitude vs. velocity), given the type of wave structure each paper studies.
CQA_362808d2bade8395.answer: The vcFLE result concerns a discrete two-body collision between localized bright solitons: because both solitons retain their individual sech-profile forms before and after interaction, the natural invariant to track is each soliton's peak amplitude, and the analysis shows Aj|+=Aj|- (Tj=1), i.e. elastic collision with amplitude preserved (only a phase shift and separation change occur). The mKdV result instead concerns the propagation of a continuous, expanding dispersive shock wave region, where there is no discrete 'before/after' amplitude to compare; instead the physically meaningful conserved quantity is the propagation speed of the transition boundary, and when the background value a is constant, the small-amplitude edge's velocity is fixed at -12a, matching the linear group velocity of the underlying dispersion relation. Thus amplitude invariance is the natural conserved quantity for particle-like soliton collisions, whereas velocity invariance is the natural conserved quantity for a continuously expanding shock-edge boundary.

CQA_a1b5b7fe4369062a.question: Both papers report a marginal average performance guarantee (coverage rate for AQCP; AUROC/balanced accuracy for AS classifiers) that can obscure poor performance on a specific slice of the data. What is the distinct statistical mechanism each paper identifies as the root cause of this marginal-conditional gap, and why does neither mechanism let the marginal guarantee alone certify conditional validity?
CQA_a1b5b7fe4369062a.answer: In the quantum conformal prediction paper, the marginal average-coverage guarantee (asymptotic in N test points) holds even under arbitrary non-stationary hardware noise, but this guarantee says nothing about coverage at any particular time slice: shots taken at different times are drawn from time-varying distributions, so the augmented observations and scores are not exchangeable across time, meaning average coverage can mask local over- or under-coverage at specific points in the stream (e.g. AQCP's baseline QCP over-covers around test points 2,000-3,000 and under-covers near point 8,500 despite eventual target average coverage). In the echocardiogram subgroup paper, the marginal-conditional gap arises instead from small subgroup sample sizes: TMED-2 has as few as 17-43 patients for Latino/Asian subgroups, so subgroup AUROC/balanced accuracy estimates carry very wide bootstrap confidence intervals (e.g. 21.1 percentage points for white patients versus 66.6-100.0 percentage points for other subgroups), making apparent subgroup disparities statistically insignificant rather than confirmed. Thus in AQCP the gap stems from a violated exchangeability/distributional-stationarity assumption over time, while in the echocardiogram case it stems from insufficient representative data per subgroup; neither marginal guarantee (average coverage, or aggregate AUROC) can be used alone to certify performance for a specific time point or specific demographic subgroup.

CQA_acd03521a9e80942.question: Both papers rely on a compact surrogate representation in place of an exact underlying model to make their PPO-trained control policies practical. What does each surrogate approximate, and what correction or design mechanism does each paper add to keep the surrogate's error from disrupting policy learning or deployment?
CQA_acd03521a9e80942.answer: In the distributed voltage regulation paper, the surrogate is the Thevenin equivalent circuit (parameters Eth, Zth) approximating the true nonlinear power-flow relationship between injected power and node voltage; because this simplified circuit has different sensitivity to control actions than the real network, the paper adds a piecewise polynomial correction function to fix large estimation errors and a Transformer-based neural network to mimic the network's true sensitivity to actions, together bringing relative voltage estimation error down to roughly ±2%. In KANELE, the surrogate is the learned KAN spline activation approximating the true policy/value mapping, which must be quantized for FPGA deployment; quantization-aware training (with straight-through estimator gradients) and norm-based pruning are used jointly during training so that the deployed low-bitwidth LUT representation matches the behavior learned in floating point, allowing the 8-bit KAN actor to still outperform the floating-point KAN and larger MLP baselines in reward. Both papers therefore pair a lightweight surrogate (Thevenin circuit or quantized spline/LUT) with a training-time correction mechanism (neural sensitivity correction or quantization-aware training) to preserve policy quality despite the surrogate's approximation error.

CQA_802ea554fcf3e9b8.question: Both papers train reinforcement learning control policies with the PPO algorithm, yet each targets a distinct computational bottleneck for real-time deployment. What is the bottleneck in each case, and what architectural substitution does each paper introduce to remove it?
CQA_802ea554fcf3e9b8.answer: In the voltage regulation paper, the bottleneck is the need for centralized power-flow (PF) calculations at every decision step, which requires synchronized smart-meter data collection across the network and induces communication overhead and privacy risk; the paper removes this by embedding a dynamic Thevenin equivalent model in each smart meter so the local RL agent can estimate voltage magnitude from local data alone, eliminating synchronized PF solves and cutting training time to about one-third of the centralized approach. In the KANELE paper, the bottleneck is the FPGA hardware cost of neural inference in the PPO policy (actor) network; the paper removes this by replacing the MLP actor with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network whose spline activations are directly instantiated as LUTs, and by 8-bit quantization, giving a ~5x parameter reduction and inference latency of 4.5 ns versus 893 ns for an 8-bit MLP actor on the HalfCheetah control task. Thus both papers resolve their real-time bottleneck by substituting the expensive shared/centralized computation (PF solve or dense matrix-multiply MLP) with a locally/structurally efficient surrogate (Thevenin-based local estimation or LUT-native KAN activations).

CQA_f221e661b4d554cf.question: Both papers train PPO policies for continuous control but embed the learned nonlinear function approximator in different parts of the pipeline. CQA_f221e661b4d554cf.answer: In the distributed voltage regulation paper, PPO trains local RL agents whose observed voltage state comes from a Thevenin-equivalent local estimate; because this simplified circuit model has different sensitivity to control actions than the real grid, a Transformer neural network (ANN0) is inserted into the local environment to model the network's true action sensitivity, correcting the state fed to the PPO policy so the agent can converge without needing synchronized centralized power-flow calculations. Thus the two works apply learned nonlinear approximators at complementary points of a PPO pipeline: one augments the state/reward-relevant sensitivity estimate to compensate for a simplified physical model, the other replaces the policy network itself to shrink the hardware footprint of the deployed controller, and both are motivated by the same objective of minimizing online computation for real-time RL-based control.

State precisely what spectral quantity sets each threshold, and explain why in both settings the threshold is the exact point at which the underlying comparison inequality (Lemma 3 in the torsion paper, the eigenvalue estimate in Proposition 2.8 of the manifold paper) ceases to guarantee the sign/positivity needed for the argument.

In the Cartan–Hadamard paper, non-existence of bounded solutions requires λ ≤ (n−1)²κ/4, i.e. λ must stay at or below (a multiple of) the bottom of the spectrum λ0 of the Laplacian on the pinched manifold; this bound is needed because the contradiction argument invokes Proposition 2.8, which forces λ ≥ λ1(D) > λ1(M) ≥ (n−1)²κ/4, so exceeding the bound removes the comparison needed to derive a contradiction. In both papers the threshold is thus exactly the spectral quantity (Steklov eigenvalue of Ω, or bottom-of-spectrum bound of the ambient manifold) beyond which the sign-preserving comparison inequality that drives the whole proof breaks down.

CQA_189c1f1fec7458b9.question: Both papers build a special function depending only on distance to a hypersurface and compare it against a model-space solution using an inequality derived from curvature/geometry bounds. Describe the shared method and the key structural difference in how the comparison inequality is derived and used in each paper.
CQA_189c1f1fec7458b9.answer: In the torsion paper, the method of parallel coordinates builds a trial function ψ(x) := φ(R2−ρ(x)) depending on the distance ρ(x) from ∂Ω, and compares its Dirichlet energy/integral to the solution u of a Dirichlet–Neumann problem on a spherical shell via the Aleksandrov–Fenchel inequality (12) applied to the level sets Et, giving |∂Et| ≤ |∂Bt| and hence τD(Ω) ≥ τDN(AR1,R2) (Theorem 5). In the manifold paper, the analogous device is a supersolution v = h∘dΣ built from the signed distance function to a convex hypersurface Σ, where h solves an ODE (3.4) linked to a curvature bound; the comparison inequality ∆v(p) ≤ h''(L)+h'(L)(n−1)√κ tanh(√κL) ≤ −λv(p) is derived via an index-form/Jacobi-field comparison with hyperbolic space (Lemma 3.1), not via an Aleksandrov–Fenchel-type isoperimetric inequality. Thus both papers reduce a hard variational/PDE estimate to a distance-function-based comparison with an explicit model solution, but the torsion paper's comparison is convexity/isoperimetric (Aleksandrov–Fenchel, static geometric inequality on level-set boundaries), while the manifold paper's comparison is curvature/Jacobi-field-based (dynamic ODE comparison along geodesics via Ricci bounds).

CQA_81e504cbc001104c.question: Both the ARLF robust regression learner and the GMQ quantile loss function use a single scalar shape parameter to interpolate between distinct loss regimes. How do the two papers differ in how this parameter governs the bias-robustness tradeoff, and can they be unified under a shared design criterion?
CQA_81e504cbc001104c.answer: Both papers parameterize a family of loss functions by one scalar that smoothly moves between a quadratic-like regime and a robust regime. ARLF's alpha degrades to the L2 (MSE) loss as alpha approaches 2, becomes the Charbonnier loss at alpha=1, and behaves as the Geman-McClure or Welsch loss as alpha decreases toward -2 or negative infinity, down-weighting large errors; alpha is treated as a learnable parameter optimized during training so the model data-adaptively selects its own robustness level. GMQ's shape parameter c interpolates between the two linear asymptotes of the check loss as c to 0 (recovering the classical, non-smooth check loss exactly at c=0) and increasing smoothing/bias as c grows; unlike ARLF's data-driven optimization, c's value is set by asymptotic theory that balances a smoothing bias of order O(c^2|lnc|) against a variance reduction of order O(c), yielding a theoretically optimal c* that scales as n^{-1/3}. Both papers thus share the criterion of a single shape scalar controlling a smoothness-versus-robustness/accuracy tradeoff, but ARLF selects it by empirical learning during optimization while GMQ selects it by an explicit asymptotic bias-variance calculation.

CQA_7a3cb6dd613b0c8a.question: Both papers face the problem that a dense, unstructured covariance matrix is computationally or statistically intractable in high dimensions; what distinct structural simplification does each use to replace full covariance inversion, and what property of the data does each simplification exploit?
CQA_7a3cb6dd613b0c8a.answer: Paper 1 replaces the full pooled sample covariance matrix Sn by its diagonal, forming Λn = (diag(Sn) + kIp)^-1, because the full Sn is ill-conditioned and inconsistent when p grows with n, while the diagonal retains the heterogeneous per-coordinate variance information needed for the test statistic. Paper 2 instead exploits the assumed spatial stationarity of the image, blur, and noise processes on a cyclic lattice: this makes the relevant covariance matrices circulant or block-circulant-with-circulant-blocks (BCCB), which are diagonalized by the (2D) discrete Fourier transform, so that covariance operations such as inversion and multiplication reduce to elementwise operations on eigenvalues computable via the FFT. Thus Paper 1's simplification trades the full cross-covariance structure for per-coordinate variances, whereas Paper 2's simplification preserves full spatial covariance structure but diagonalizes it via stationarity and the Fourier basis rather than discarding off-diagonal information.
CQA_7a3cb6dd613b0c8a.relation: Paper 1 alone only shows the diagonal-replacement strategy under linear-rate high-dimensional asymptotics; Paper 2 alone only shows the circulant/BCCB Fourier-diagonalization strategy under spatial stationarity. Comparing the two requires both texts to identify them as two distinct families of structured covariance approximation solving the same underlying tractability problem.
CQA_7a3cb6dd613b0c8a.derived_conclusion: High-dimensional covariance intractability can be resolved either by discarding off-diagonal covariance entirely (Paper 1's diagonal approach, suited to unstructured heterogeneous variances) or by retaining full covariance structure but diagonalizing it through an assumed stationary/circulant symmetry (Paper 2's Fourier approach, suited to spatially structured data).

This "structured approximation of the covariance operator" trick — trading exact full-rank matrix estimation for a computationally cheap diagonal/decomposed surrogate — is the key mechanism both papers use to scale Bayesian procedures to the p≫n or p/n→c regime while maintaining stability and controlled error rates.

CQA_446280f4f5e1c556.question: In paper 1's continuous-discrete constrained Bayesian filtering, the barrier-constrained kernel is applied recursively at each observation time to approximate the constrained transition ˆK_n from the underlying SDE. Could paper 2's discretization approximation (DA), which evaluates a density at a fixed support-point set to build a discrete approximating measure, be substituted for this recursive constrained-kernel step, and why or why not?
CQA_446280f4f5e1c556.answer: No. Paper 1's constrained kernel ˆK_n(x',·) is a transition density conditioned jointly on an initial state x' from the previous step and a terminal compact constraint set C_n, implemented via a barrier-modified SDE that must be re-simulated at every observation time as new data arrive (merged pages 11-13). DA is built for a single static target density known up to a normalizing constant: it lays a fixed support-point set A_M once and computes discrete probability masses from density evaluations at those points (merged pages 30-31), with no built-in mechanism for conditioning on a moving initial point or for refreshing support points online as observations accumulate. Moreover DA's accuracy is governed by the discrepancy δ_M,d of the point set, which for a standard sequence like Halton grows as C_d(log M)^d/M (merged page 32), so matching fixed accuracy at every one of many recursive filtering steps in a high-dimensional state space would require M to grow with dimension at each time index -- exactly the cost paper 1 avoids by truncating the state's support with compact sets C_n rather than covering the whole space with points (merged pages 8-9, 17-18). Hence DA cannot directly replace the recursive constrained-kernel machinery of paper 1's filter without abandoning its deterministic, non-recursive point-discretization design.

CQA_8070262676234f68.question: Paper 1's approximation-error bounds for constrained filters are expressed via a constraint-tightness parameter ε^l, while paper 2's discretization-approximation error is expressed via a point-set discrepancy δ_M,d. What common structural role do these two quantities play in bounding approximation error, and what is the key difference in how each is driven toward its limiting value?
CQA_8070262676234f68.answer: In both papers the error bound has the form 'constant times a single scalar governing parameter,' and that parameter is driven to a limit that recovers the exact target distribution. In paper 1, sup_{|f|≤1}|π_n(f)-π̂_n^l(f)| ≤ c(1-ε^l)/ε^l, where ε^l lower-bounds the probability mass the compact constraint set C_n^l captures from the unconstrained transition kernel, and ε^l→1 as the constraint is relaxed toward the full state space (l→∞) (merged pages 9-10). In paper 2, d_K(µ_(f,A_M), µ_f) ≤ Cδ_M,d, where δ_M,d is the discrepancy of the quasi-Monte Carlo support-point set A_M, and δ_M,d→0 as the number of points M→∞ for fixed dimension (merged pages 31-32). Both bounds require added regularity to become uniform or improved (Assumptions 3.5 and 3.7 for stable filters in paper 1; finite Hardy-Krause variation V(f)<∞ in paper 2). The key difference: ε^l measures how much probability mass a spatial truncation of the kernel retains -- a property of the dynamics restricted to a shrinking excluded region -- whereas δ_M,d measures how uniformly a fixed number of deterministic points cover the entire support -- a property of the point set's geometric spread. Refining paper 1's approximation means enlarging (relaxing) a spatial restriction toward the full space, while refining paper 2's means adding more space-filling points to densify coverage; one approaches the target by shrinking an excluded region to nothing, the other by growing a point cloud to fill the space.

Their barrier-constrained and barrier-guided filters mitigate this by restricting sampling to high-likelihood compact sets, remaining stable even as d_x grows to thousands, so their superiority claim is fairly general across dimension as long as particle/ensemble size scales at least linearly with d_x (N=⌊0.75 d_x⌋), though it is not free (accuracy still shows mild degradation, e.g. NMSE increasing slightly with d_x in Table 1). The bottleneck is therefore tied to the sampling/proposal mechanism's ability to hit the constraint region, not to the Monte Carlo estimator's intrinsic variance. This implies each paper's superiority claim is scoped to different dimension-dependent failure modes: Paper 1's alternative outperforms standard MC-based filters specifically because it avoids importance-weight collapse in state space, so its advantage should generalize to any high-dimensional filtering problem where particle degeneracy is the limiting factor, but not necessarily to settings where the bottleneck is a different one (e.g., integration-variance growth of a quasi/multilevel Monte Carlo estimator, as would be the case in a generic high-dimensional integration paper). CQA_9ace5ae0c7b94d1d.question: Both papers guarantee that the optimal control/policy selection is unique despite a structurally more complex objective. What distinct mathematical mechanism does each paper use to secure this uniqueness, and how do the two mechanisms differ in what they act on (a derived scalar reward-rate function versus the Hamiltonian itself)?
CQA_9ace5ae0c7b94d1d.answer: In the impulse control paper, uniqueness of the optimal (w*,y*) reset pair is obtained by showing the auxiliary function h(x)=(γg'(x)+p)/ξ'(x) is strictly increasing on (a, ŷ) and strictly decreasing on (ŷ,b), a single-crossing (single-peak) property that follows from the concavity/monotonicity Condition 2.6 on μ and c; this pins down a unique extremal point ŷ where h'(ŷ)=0 and hence a unique maximizing pair for the fractional payoff F. In the model-mismatch control paper, uniqueness of the pointwise-optimal control u is instead obtained by proving the Hamiltonian H(t,x,x̂,u,λ) is strongly convex in the control variable u itself (via Assumption 3's r_min-bounded quadratic control-cost term and coercivity from Assumption 4), so that the argmin over the convex admissible set U is a singleton for almost every t. Thus paper 1 enforces uniqueness through monotonicity/single-crossing behavior of a scalar function of the state threshold, while paper 2 enforces it through strong convexity of the Hamiltonian in the control variable directly.
CQA_9ace5ae0c7b94d1d.relation: Each paper's uniqueness proof is a self-contained bridge fact; comparing the two requires identifying which object (the reward-rate function h vs. the Hamiltonian H) is shown to be monotone/convex and why, so no single paper's fact alone answers the question.
CQA_9ace5ae0c7b94d1d.derived_conclusion: The two papers achieve uniqueness of optimal control through structurally different but functionally analogous devices: single-crossing monotonicity of a state-threshold function in paper 1, versus strong convexity of the control-dependent Hamiltonian in paper 2.

CQA_e64f6170bd13be74.question: Both papers include a cost/parameter component that shifts the overall value of the control problem yet does not alter the pointwise rule used to select the optimal control/threshold. Identify this component in each paper and explain the shared structural reason it is 'inert' with respect to the selection rule.
CQA_e64f6170bd13be74.answer: In the impulse control paper, the fixed intervention cost K appears in the payoff F(w,y) and in the QVI balance equation (γBg+pBi−F*Bξ=K), shifting the optimal value F* and threshold locations, but the auxiliary function h(x)=(γg'(x)+p)/ξ'(x), which characterizes optimizing pairs via h(w*)=h(y*)=F*, does not depend on K at all (the text notes explicitly that h does not involve the parameter K). In the model-mismatch control paper, the mismatch penalty β(t)‖x(t)−x̂(t)‖² is added to the model-based cost and Hamiltonian H(t,x,x̂,u,λ), shaping the state and costate trajectories, but because it does not depend on u at fixed t, it drops out of the pointwise Hamiltonian minimization/subdifferential with respect to u. In both cases the inert term is additively separable from the control/threshold variable that indexes the pointwise optimality condition, so it can affect trajectories and attained value without altering the rule that selects the optimal action.
CQA_e64f6170bd13be74.relation: Recognizing the shared 'inert term' pattern requires pairing paper 1's explicit statement that h excludes K with paper 1's balance equation showing K still affects value, and pairing this with paper 2's explicit statement that the penalty term is absent from the control gradient though present in the Hamiltonian and state/costate dynamics.
CQA_e64f6170bd13be74.derived_conclusion: Both models exhibit the same structural phenomenon: a cost component that is additively separable from the control/threshold variable influences the attained value and trajectories but is analytically invisible to the first-order rule that determines the optimal control or threshold.

CQA_6fbae8563a2b55c7.question: Both papers establish that a directly computable but 'approximate' or 'restricted' control policy converges to, or coincides with, the optimum of a harder/true problem. What is the shared logical template behind these convergence/coincidence results, and what does each paper require to make the argument work?
CQA_6fbae8563a2b55c7.answer: Both papers use the same two-step template: (1) identify a scalar function whose maximizer/minimizer over the control determines the true optimum of the harder problem (h(x) whose maximizer ŷ solves the singular control problem in Paper 1; the Hamiltonian H(t,x,x̂,u,λ) whose minimizer over u solves the model-based problem in Paper 2), and (2) show that the restricted/approximate policy's own optimality condition, in the appropriate limit or under a matching hypothesis, forces its argument to satisfy that same scalar condition. In Paper 1, the impulse policy's first-order condition h(w*_K)=h(y*_K)=F*_K forces both endpoints toward ŷ as K↓0, because h is strictly increasing then strictly decreasing with unique maximizer ŷ (Lemma 4.8), so bracketing forces convergence. In Paper 2, Theorem 3 shows that if the u-gradients of the plant and model Hamiltonians coincide at u°(t) (via matching ∇_uf̂ and λ°=x̂, x°=x̂*), then since both Hamiltonians are strictly convex in u with a unique minimizer (Lemma 1), u°(t) must equal the plant's unique minimizer u*(t). In both cases, convergence/coincidence is not obtained by matching the underlying dynamics or cost structure but by forcing the approximate policy's stationarity point to fall into the same uniqueness class (unique maximizer of h; unique minimizer of a strictly convex Hamiltonian) as the true optimum.

CQA_6fbae8563a2b55c7.derived_conclusion: Convergence of an impulse policy to the singular optimum, and coincidence of a model-based control with the plant-optimal control, are both instances of forcing a restricted policy's first-order condition into the basin of a uniquely characterized stationary point of a governing scalar/Hamiltonian function.

intermediate_facts.fact: Lemma 4.7/4.8 establish that h=γh_c+ph_μ is strictly increasing then strictly decreasing on I, giving a unique maximizer.
ŷ is defined as min{x∈I: h'(x)=0}, the unique smallest critical point of h.
Proposition 7.1 proof shows h(w*_K)=h(y*_K)=F*_K→h(ŷ) as K↓0, forcing both w*_K and y*_K to converge to ŷ.
The convergence of the (w*_K,y*_K)-impulse policy to the Z_ŷ singular policy is established as a direct consequence of this squeeze argument.
Theorem 1 establishes that under strict convexity, the pointwise Hamiltonian minimizer over U is unique for almost every t.
Lemma 1's proof uses coercivity and strong convexity from the quadratic control term to guarantee a unique minimizer even on unbounded U.
Theorem 3 shows that if the plant and model Hamiltonian gradients coincide at u°(t), the variational inequality forces u°(t) to be the (unique) minimizer of the plant Hamiltonian.
Because this unique minimizer set is a singleton {u*}, u°(t)=u*(t) follows directly from the matching condition.

CQA_6fbae8563a2b55c7.answer_pre: {"answer_pre":"Both papers use the same verification template: (1) restrict attention to a directly computable, explicitly parametrized policy class (here the (w,y)-impulse policies of Definition 3.1, with reward rate F(w,y) computed in closed form via a renewal argument, eq. (3.3)); (2) using the maximizer (w*,y*) of this restricted objective, construct an auxiliary potential/value function (G(x)=F*ξ(x)-γg(x), eq. (4.10)) that solves the associated Bellman-type quasi-variational inequality AG+γc-F*≤0, with equality attained exactly at the (w*,y*)-policy; (3) apply Itô's formula/Dynkin's formula to this potential along an arbitrary admissible policy R to get a pathwise inequality (4.16)-(4.17) bounding the long-term average reward J(R) above by F*; (4) pass to the long-time limit and use a transversality/boundedness condition (the limsup-liminf condition (2.6)/(4.13), proved via Fatou's lemma) to kill the boundary/potential term so the inequality survives in the limit. The conclusion J(R) ≤ F* = F(w*,y*) for every admissible R, combined with the fact that the (w*,y*)-policy itself attains F*, establishes that the explicitly computable (w*,y*)-policy is globally optimal over the full admissible class A. What each paper needs to make this work is: existence and uniqueness of the maximizing pair (w*,y*) for the restricted fractional-optimization functional F (Propositions 4.2, 4.9, requiring Conditions 2.1, 2.5, 2.6, 4.1 on the diffusion, running reward, and profitability of intervening), monotonicity of the potential G, and the transversality condition (2.6)/(4.13) that guarantees the boundary term in the Itô expansion vanishes in the long-run average limit — without this transversality condition the verification argument fails to close for admissible policies with infinitely many interventions.","evidence_pages":[14,15,16,17,18,19,20]}

CQA_6fbae8563a2b55c7.prediction_answer: Both papers use the same verification template: (1) restrict attention to a directly computable, explicitly parametrized policy class (here the (w,y)-impulse policies of Definition 3.1, with reward rate F(w,y) computed in closed form via a renewal argument, eq. (3.3)); (2) using the maximizer (w*,y*) of this restricted objective, construct an auxiliary potential/value function (G(x)=F*ξ(x)-γg(x), eq. (4.10)) that solves the associated Bellman-type quasi-variational inequality AG+γc-F*≤0, with equality attained exactly at the (w*,y*)-policy; (3) apply Itô's formula/Dynkin's formula to this potential along an arbitrary admissible policy R to get a pathwise inequality (4.16)-(4.17) bounding the long-term average reward J(R) above by F*; (4) pass to the long-time limit and use a transversality/boundedness condition (the limsup-liminf condition (2.6)/(4.13), proved via Fatou's lemma) to kill the boundary/potential term so the inequality survives in the limit. The conclusion J(R) ≤ F* = F(w*,y*) for every admissible R, combined with the fact that the (w*,y*)-policy itself attains F*, establishes that the explicitly computable (w*,y*)-policy is globally optimal over the full admissible class A. What each paper needs to make this work is: existence and uniqueness of the maximizing pair (w*,y*) for the restricted fractional-optimization functional F (Propositions 4.2, 4.9, requiring Conditions 2.1, 2.5, 2.6, 4.1 on the diffusion, running reward, and profitability of intervening), monotonicity of the potential G, and the transversality condition (2.6)/(4.13) that guarantees the boundary term in the Itô expansion vanishes in the long-run average limit — without this transversality condition the verification argument fails to close for admissible policies with infinitely many interventions.
